# Differential expression with DESeq2 and edgeR {#sec-de}

We now ask which genes change in expression when TDP-43 is knocked down. The
main tool is DESeq2 [@love2014]; edgeR's quasi-likelihood pipeline
[@robinson2010; @chen2016] serves as a second method that is often preferred
for small sample sizes. At the end we look at what happens if the batch had
not been recorded, using surrogate variable analysis [@leek2014].

```{r}
#| label: setup
source("R/helpers.R")
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(DESeq2)
  library(edgeR)
  library(sva)
  library(dplyr)
  library(ggplot2)
})
fmt_p <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1)
```

## The comparison

From @sec-design and @sec-qc we take three decisions:

- **Samples**: TDP-43 siRNA (n = 6) versus scramble siRNA (n = 6).
- **Model**: `~ batch + condition`, because batch is the largest source of
  variation and is balanced across groups.
- **Reference level**: scramble, so that positive log2 fold changes mean
  *higher in the knockdown*.

```{r}
#| label: subset
rse <- load_counts_rse()
rse <- rse[, rse$sirna %in% c("scramble", "TDP43")]
rse$condition <- droplevels(rse$sirna)
rse$batch <- droplevels(rse$batch)
table(condition = rse$condition, batch = rse$batch)
```

## Setting the reference level explicitly

R orders factor levels alphabetically unless told otherwise. Here that would
happen to give the right answer ("scramble" before "TDP43"), but relying on
alphabetical order is fragile: name the groups "WT" and "KD" and the
knockdown silently becomes the reference, flipping the sign of every fold
change. We therefore always set the
reference with `relevel()`.

```{r}
#| label: relevel
rse$condition <- relevel(factor(rse$condition), ref = "scramble")
levels(rse$condition)
```

## Filtering low counts

Genes with very few reads carry almost no information and add to the
multiple-testing burden. Our rule: **at least 10 counts in at least as many
samples as the smallest group** (here 6). The rule ignores the group labels,
so it cannot bias the test towards one group.

```{r}
#| label: dds
dds <- DESeqDataSet(rse, design = ~ batch + condition)
min_group <- min(table(dds$condition))
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds) >= 10) >= min_group
dds <- dds[keep, ]
c(smallest_group = min_group, genes_tested = nrow(dds))
```

## Fitting the model

`DESeq()` estimates size factors (library size normalisation), fits one
dispersion per gene with shrinkage towards a trend, and fits a negative
binomial GLM for each gene.

```{r}
#| label: deseq
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dispersion
#| fig-cap: "Dispersion estimates. Black: per-gene estimates; red: fitted trend; blue: final shrunken estimates. Circled points are outliers kept at their own estimate."
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
plotDispEsts(dds)
```

The dispersion plot is a quick health check: estimates should scatter around
a smooth decreasing trend, as they do here.

## Results: raw and shrunken fold changes

`results()` gives the maximum likelihood log2 fold change, its standard
error, and a Wald test p-value adjusted for multiple testing with the
Benjamini-Hochberg method (padj).

For genes with few counts, the raw log2 fold change can be very large simply
because of noise. `lfcShrink()` with the apeglm prior [@zhu2019] pulls noisy
estimates towards zero while leaving well-supported large effects almost
untouched. We use the **shrunken** values for ranking and plots, and keep
the **raw** values in the table as well, in separate, clearly named columns.

```{r}
#| label: results
coef_name <- "condition_TDP43_vs_scramble"
res <- results(dds, name = coef_name, alpha = DE_PADJ)
res_shr <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = coef_name, type = "apeglm", quiet = TRUE)
summary(res)
```

```{r}
#| label: result-table
de <- data.frame(
  gene_id        = rownames(res),
  symbol         = rowData(dds)$gene_name,
  gene_type      = rowData(dds)$gene_type,
  baseMean       = res$baseMean,
  log2FC         = res$log2FoldChange,      # raw (MLE)
  lfcSE          = res$lfcSE,               # raw (MLE)
  log2FC_shrunk  = res_shr$log2FoldChange,  # apeglm
  lfcSE_shrunk   = res_shr$lfcSE,           # apeglm
  stat           = res$stat,
  pvalue         = res$pvalue,
  padj           = res$padj
) |>
  arrange(padj)
```

## Calling differentially expressed genes

Our predefined thresholds are **padj < 0.05** and **|log2FC| > 1**. We apply
the fold change cut-off to the shrunken estimate, so that a gene cannot pass
only because its raw fold change is inflated by noise.

```{r}
#| label: call-de
de <- de |>
  mutate(DE = case_when(
    !is.na(padj) & padj < DE_PADJ & log2FC_shrunk >  DE_LFC ~ "up",
    !is.na(padj) & padj < DE_PADJ & log2FC_shrunk < -DE_LFC ~ "down",
    TRUE ~ "not significant"))
table(de$DE)
```

```{r}
#| label: top-table
de |>
  filter(DE != "not significant") |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(across(c(baseMean, log2FC, lfcSE, log2FC_shrunk, lfcSE_shrunk), \(x) round(x, 2)),
         across(c(pvalue, padj), fmt_p)) |>
  select(gene_id, symbol, baseMean, log2FC, lfcSE, log2FC_shrunk, pvalue, padj, DE) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

Of the `r sum(de$padj < DE_PADJ, na.rm = TRUE)` genes with padj < 0.05, only
`r sum(de$DE != "not significant")` also change more than two-fold. Most
responses to a partial TDP-43 knockdown are modest, which is why the fold
change threshold has to be fixed in advance: a slightly different cut-off
would change the list a lot, and choosing it after seeing the result would
make the list meaningless.

*TARDBP* itself should be among the most significant genes, and it is. Next
to it in the table are two other GENCODE v26 genes annotated on top of the
*TARDBP* locus: RP4-635E18.9, whose exons overlap *TARDBP*, and RP4-635E18.8,
just downstream of it. recount3 counts a read for every gene whose exons it
covers, so genes that share sequence with the siRNA target drop together with
it. They are not independent findings. *STMN2* is
also strongly reduced, while *UNC13A* and *POLDIP3* do not change at the gene
level. For *UNC13A* that is not evidence against a splicing effect; we come
back to it in @sec-cryptic.

```{r}
#| label: known-genes
de |>
  filter(symbol %in% c("TARDBP", "STMN2", "UNC13A", "POLDIP3")) |>
  mutate(across(c(baseMean, log2FC, log2FC_shrunk), \(x) round(x, 2)),
         across(c(pvalue, padj), fmt_p)) |>
  select(symbol, baseMean, log2FC, log2FC_shrunk, padj, DE) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## A formal test against a fold change threshold
Filtering on |log2FC| after testing against zero is common practice, but the
padj then refers to "any change", not to "a change larger than 2-fold". If
you need the latter, DESeq2 can test it directly with
`results(dds, lfcThreshold = 1)`. Here this gives
`r sum(results(dds, name = coef_name, lfcThreshold = 1, alpha = DE_PADJ)$padj < DE_PADJ, na.rm = TRUE)`
genes, compared with `r sum(de$DE != "not significant")` from the filter
approach. Report which approach you used.
:::

```{r}
#| label: save
write.csv(de, "results/de_deseq2_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv", row.names = FALSE)
saveRDS(dds, cache_path("dds_TDP43_vs_scramble.rds"))
write.csv(as.data.frame(counts(dds, normalized = TRUE)) |>
            tibble::rownames_to_column("gene_id"),
          gzfile(cache_path("normalized_counts.csv.gz")), row.names = FALSE)
```

The full table is saved as `results/de_deseq2_TDP43_vs_scramble.csv`.

## edgeR quasi-likelihood: a second opinion

With only a handful of replicates per group, the quasi-likelihood (QL)
F-test in edgeR is a good alternative: it accounts for the uncertainty in
estimating each gene's dispersion and tends to be conservative. We use the
same genes and the same design so that the two methods can be compared
directly.

```{r}
#| label: edger
y <- DGEList(counts = counts(dds), samples = as.data.frame(colData(dds)[, c("condition", "batch")]))
y <- normLibSizes(y)                               # TMM normalisation
design <- model.matrix(~ batch + condition, data = y$samples)
fit <- glmQLFit(y, design)
qlf <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef = "conditionTDP43")
et <- topTags(qlf, n = Inf, sort.by = "none")$table
edger <- data.frame(gene_id = rownames(et), logFC = et$logFC, PValue = et$PValue, FDR = et$FDR)
edger$DE <- with(edger, ifelse(FDR < DE_PADJ & abs(logFC) > DE_LFC,
                               ifelse(logFC > 0, "up", "down"), "not significant"))
table(edger$DE)
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-methods
cmp <- inner_join(de, edger, by = "gene_id", suffix = c(".deseq2", ".edger"))
sig_d <- cmp$gene_id[cmp$DE.deseq2 != "not significant"]
sig_e <- cmp$gene_id[cmp$DE.edger  != "not significant"]
both <- intersect(sig_d, sig_e)
data.frame(
  DESeq2_only = length(setdiff(sig_d, sig_e)),
  both        = length(both),
  edgeR_only  = length(setdiff(sig_e, sig_d)),
  same_direction_in_both = mean(sign(cmp$log2FC[cmp$gene_id %in% both]) ==
                                sign(cmp$logFC[cmp$gene_id %in% both])),
  spearman_logFC_all_genes = cor(cmp$log2FC, cmp$logFC, method = "spearman")
)
```

Both methods call largely the same genes
(`r length(both)` shared, `r length(setdiff(sig_d, sig_e))` DESeq2 only,
`r length(setdiff(sig_e, sig_d))` edgeR only), every shared gene changes in
the same direction, and the fold changes of all tested genes are almost
perfectly rank-correlated. edgeR calls more genes here mainly because we
applied the fold change cut-off to the *shrunken* DESeq2 estimate but to the
unshrunken edgeR estimate. Genes called by only one method sit close to a
threshold in both; they are a reminder that a cut-off is a convention, not a
property of the gene.

## What if the batch had not been recorded?

Suppose the dates were missing from the metadata. PCA would still show two
clusters of samples, but we would not know why. Surrogate variable analysis
(svaseq) estimates hidden factors from the data, and these can be added to
the model in place of the unknown batch.

Two rules apply whenever you use it:

1. **Report the number of surrogate variables (SVs)** and how it was chosen.
2. **Report a sensitivity check**: how many genes pass the thresholds with
   and without the SVs, how many overlap, and whether the direction agrees.

```{r}
#| label: svaseq
dds_nobatch <- DESeqDataSet(rse[rownames(dds), ], design = ~ condition)
dds_nobatch <- estimateSizeFactors(dds_nobatch)
norm_counts <- counts(dds_nobatch, normalized = TRUE)
mod  <- model.matrix(~ condition, colData(dds_nobatch))
mod0 <- model.matrix(~ 1, colData(dds_nobatch))
n_sv <- num.sv(log2(norm_counts + 1), mod, method = "be", seed = 1)
set.seed(1)
sv <- svaseq(norm_counts, mod, mod0, n.sv = n_sv)$sv
colnames(sv) <- paste0("SV", seq_len(ncol(sv)))
n_sv
```

The permutation-based method ("be") suggests `r n_sv` surrogate
variable(s). Does the first one recover the batch we hid?

```{r}
#| label: sv-vs-batch
round(cor(sv, as.numeric(dds_nobatch$batch == "B2")), 2)
```

Now fit three models on the same genes and compare them.

```{r}
#| label: sva-sensitivity
fit_calls <- function(d) {
  d <- DESeq(d, quiet = TRUE)
  cf <- "condition_TDP43_vs_scramble"
  r <- results(d, name = cf, alpha = DE_PADJ)
  s <- lfcShrink(d, coef = cf, type = "apeglm", quiet = TRUE)
  data.frame(gene_id = rownames(r), lfc = s$log2FoldChange, padj = r$padj,
             sig = !is.na(r$padj) & r$padj < DE_PADJ & abs(s$log2FoldChange) > DE_LFC)
}
colData(dds_nobatch) <- cbind(colData(dds_nobatch), sv)
sv_formula <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(colnames(sv), collapse = " + "), "+ condition"))
models <- list(
  batch_known = de |> transmute(gene_id, lfc = log2FC_shrunk, padj,
                                sig = DE != "not significant"),
  no_adjustment = fit_calls(DESeqDataSet(rse[rownames(dds), ], design = ~ condition)),
  svaseq = fit_calls(DESeqDataSet(SummarizedExperiment(
    assays = list(counts = counts(dds_nobatch)), colData = colData(dds_nobatch)),
    design = sv_formula))
)
ref <- models$batch_known
sens <- lapply(names(models), function(m) {
  x <- inner_join(ref, models[[m]], by = "gene_id", suffix = c(".ref", ".m"))
  shared <- x$sig.ref & x$sig.m
  data.frame(model = m,
             genes_passing = sum(x$sig.m),
             overlap_with_batch_model = sum(shared),
             same_direction = if (any(shared)) mean(sign(x$lfc.ref[shared]) == sign(x$lfc.m[shared])) else NA)
})
do.call(rbind, sens) |> knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

How to read this table:

- **no_adjustment** ignores the batch completely. Because batch was the
  largest source of variation, leaving it out inflates the residual
  variance, so only `r sens[[2]]$genes_passing` genes pass, all of them also
  found by the batch model.
- **svaseq** used `r n_sv` surrogate variables. The first one is almost the
  hidden batch (correlation `r round(cor(sv[, 1], as.numeric(dds_nobatch$batch == "B2")), 2)`).
  It finds `r sens[[3]]$genes_passing` genes, of which
  `r sens[[3]]$overlap_with_batch_model` are shared with the known-batch
  model, all with the same direction. These three numbers (genes passing,
  overlap, direction agreement) are the sensitivity check you report.
- The `r sens[[3]]$genes_passing - sens[[3]]$overlap_with_batch_model`
  genes found only with SVs are not "extra discoveries". They show that
  the SVs also absorb some variation that is not batch, which changes the
  result at the margin.

::: {.callout-warning}
## When not to use SVA
If the batch is known, model it directly, as we did. Surrogate variables can
absorb part of the biological signal when the hidden factor is correlated
with the condition, and they make the model harder to explain. SVA is a
tool for unknown structure, not a replacement for recording your batches.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding
1. What would change in the results table if you forgot `relevel()` and the
   groups were named "WT" and "KD"?
2. Why do we apply the |log2FC| cut-off to the shrunken rather than the raw
   fold change?
3. The filter keeps genes with at least 10 counts in at least 6 samples. Why
   6, and why is this filter not biased towards either group?
4. You used svaseq and found 3 SVs. What else must you report?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. "KD" sorts before "WT", so the knockdown would become the reference and
   every log2 fold change would flip sign, with no warning. `relevel()`
   removes the dependency on spelling.
2. Raw fold changes of low-count genes are noisy and can be large by chance.
   Shrinkage keeps large, well-supported effects and pulls noisy ones towards
   zero, so the cut-off selects genes with reliable large effects.
3. 6 is the size of the smallest group, so a gene expressed in only one group
   can still pass. The rule does not look at group labels, so it is
   independent of the test statistic under the null hypothesis.
4. How the number was chosen, and a sensitivity analysis: genes passing with
   and without SVs, their overlap, and the direction agreement.
:::
:::
